passage: I'm Gurleen, and my roommate Mridul lost his father in June. By November I had stopped telling myself it was only grief. Mridul hadn't been to a lecture in weeks, slept through the afternoons and left plates untouched on the desk we shared. What frightened me most was one night when he said, flatly, "Everyone would be better off without me." I sat down on his bed. My heart was hammering, but I asked him straight out whether he was thinking of not living. He said, "Sometimes." I told him I was glad he'd told me and that I wasn't leaving the room. We called the campus crisis line together, and the next morning I walked with him to the counsellor. She said grief and depression can arrive together, and that getting help wasn't a betrayal of his dad. He still misses his father. But he's getting help now, and he's back in class.

qa.q: When did Mridul's father die?
qa.a: In June.

qa.q: How did Gurleen feel when asking Mridul the direct question, and what shows it?
qa.a: Gurleen was frightened; Gurleen's heart was hammering, yet the question was still asked plainly.

qa.q: What choice did Gurleen make after Mridul said "Sometimes", and why was it right?
qa.a: Gurleen stayed in the room, called the campus crisis line with Mridul and walked him to the counsellor next morning, so he was not alone and got professional help.

qa.q: How might Mridul have felt when Gurleen asked him straight out?
qa.a: He may have felt some relief at being asked plainly, which made it easier for him to admit how bad things were.

grounding: It shows a roommate noticing, months after a death, that grief has turned into not functioning and talk of not wanting to live, and encouraging professional help.

passage:
Supervisor's note, bakery kitchen, 14 February. Written by Rashmi.
Uday's mother died last June. For months he worked through it quietly, and I let him keep her photo in the locker room. Lately it is different. He has come in late nine times this month, forgot the ovens twice and stands staring at the dough. Today he said, "I'm useless at everything now. It won't ever get better." That sounded bigger than missing her.
What I did next: I took him to the back office and said I was worried about him, not about the bread. I asked plainly whether he had thoughts of ending his life. He said no, only that everything feels heavy. I told him grief and low mood can come together, and that a doctor or counsellor could help. We looked up the free counselling clinic near the station together, and he booked for Friday. I gave him that morning off.

qa.q: How many times has Uday come in late this month?
qa.a: Nine times.

qa.q: Why was Rashmi worried that Uday's words were bigger than missing his mother?
qa.a: Rashmi felt alarmed because he called himself useless at everything and said it won't ever get better, which sounded like hopelessness beyond the loss.

qa.q: Which step by Rashmi turned worry into action?
qa.a: Rashmi asked plainly about thoughts of ending his life, then looked up the free counselling clinic with Uday so he could book a visit, with that morning off.

qa.q: What might it be like for Uday to hear that Rashmi was worried about him, not the bread?
qa.a: He may feel seen as a person rather than a failing worker, which makes accepting help easier.

grounding: It shows a supervisor noticing that months after a loss a young worker cannot function and feels worthless, and encouraging professional help.

passage:
Thursday night, late
It's been eight months since Jeevan's mother died. At first he cried, then he started coming back to class. But these last weeks he's stopped attending, stopped eating in the mess, sleeps all day. Today he said, "I'm worthless without her. I don't want to live."
I didn't leave. I sat right there on his floor and said, "Thank you for telling me. I'm staying." I called the student helpline on speaker with him. Then, with his okay, I called his elder sister, who's driving over tonight, and the warden came up. I'm still in the corridor outside his door, writing this.
Tomorrow at ten we're going to the counselling centre together. Grief and depression can come together, the helpline person said.
Lakshmi

qa.q: How long ago did Jeevan's mother die?
qa.a: Eight months ago.

qa.q: How was Lakshmi feeling when Jeevan said he didn't want to live?
qa.a: Lakshmi was frightened but steady, determined to stay and keep him safe.

qa.q: What did Lakshmi do that was right?
qa.a: Lakshmi stayed with him, called the helpline with him right then, called his sister and the warden that night, and arranged counselling for the next morning.

qa.q: How might Jeevan have felt when Lakshmi said she was staying?
qa.a: He may have felt less alone and a little safer, knowing someone would not leave him.

grounding: Shows a supporter noticing that months after a loss a friend cannot function, feels worthless and speaks of not wanting to live, and getting professional help at once.

passage: Nearly a year after their father died, Hansa found her brother Hrithik, twenty-two, still in bed at noon. The wheat was ready, and he hadn't been to the field in weeks. He barely ate. When she sat down he said, "What use am I? I can't even do Papa's work. Everyone would do better without me here." Hansa's chest went cold. She didn't argue or scold. "Hrithik, I'm so glad you told me. I'm not leaving you alone." She held his hand, called Ma in from the courtyard, and they stayed with him. That evening Hansa called the helpline number from the health centre poster. The next morning they took the bus to the district hospital to see the doctor together.

qa.q: What crop was ready?
qa.a: The wheat was ready.

qa.q: How did Hansa feel when Hrithik spoke?
qa.a: Her chest went cold with fear, but she stayed calm and caring.

qa.q: What did Hansa do that shows a wise response?
qa.a: She stayed with him, called Ma in at once, called a helpline that evening and took him to the doctor the next morning.

qa.q: How might Ma feel when Hansa calls her in?
qa.a: Ma is likely frightened and heartbroken but grateful that Hansa noticed and acted at once.

grounding: Shows a supporter noticing that long after a loss her brother cannot function, feels worthless and hopeless, and getting professional help at once.

passage:
Five months after his mother's funeral in Osaka, Kaito had stopped going to lectures. His flat smelled of old takeaway. Leila, his classmate, came by with notes and found him still in bed at two in the afternoon.
"I'm useless," he said. "I can't do anything. And honestly, I don't see the point of living without her."
Leila put the notes down and sat on the floor by the bed. Her heart was pounding. "Kaito, thank you for telling me. Are you thinking about ending your life?"
"Sometimes."
"Then I'm staying with you, and we're calling the university counselling line right now. Together."
He didn't argue. She dialled on speaker and stayed while he talked. The counsellor arranged an urgent appointment that afternoon. Leila walked him there. On the way she said, "Missing her this much makes sense. But this heaviness needs more than just time."

qa.q: What time did Leila find Kaito still in bed?
qa.a: At two in the afternoon.

qa.q: How was Kaito feeling five months after the funeral?
qa.a: He felt hopeless and worthless, unable to function, and said he didn't see the point of living without his mother.

qa.q: Why was Leila's response the right one?
qa.a: She took his words seriously, asked directly, stayed with him and got professional help that same afternoon instead of waiting.

qa.q: What was it like for Leila when Kaito said he didn't see the point of living?
qa.a: She was frightened, with her heart pounding, but she stayed calm and present for him.

grounding: Leila notices Kaito months after his loss cannot function and speaks of not wanting to live, and she stays and gets him professional help at once.
